section.heading: 4.6 Change of Basis
section.paragraph: When a basis $$B$$ is chosen for an $$n$$ -dimensional vector space $$V$$ , the associated coordinate mapping onto $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ provides a coordinate system for $$V$$ . Each $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ is identified uniquely by its $$B$$ -coordinate vector $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ .1

In some applications, a problem is described initially using a basis $$B$$ , but the problem’s solution is aided by changing $$B$$ to a new basis $$C$$ . (Examples will be given in Chapters 5 and 7.) Each vector is assigned a new $$C$$ -coordinate vector. In this section, we study how $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{C}$$ and $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ are related for each $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ .

To visualize the problem, consider the two coordinate systems in Figure 1. In Figure 1(a), $$\mathbf{x} = 3\mathbf{b}_{1} + \mathbf{b}_{2}$$ , while in Figure 1(b), the same $$\mathbf{x}$$ is shown as $$\mathbf{x} = 6\mathbf{c}_{1} + 4\mathbf{c}_{2}$$ . That is,

$$\left(\left[\right. x \left]\right.\right)_{B} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \text{and} & \left(\left[\right. x \left]\right.\right)_{C} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}6 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

section.paragraph: The columns of $$\underset{C\leftarrow B}{P}$$ are linearly independent because they are the coordinate vectors of the linearly independent set $$B$$ . (See Exercise 29 in Section 4.4.) Since $$\underset{C\leftarrow B}{P}$$ is square, it must be invertible, by the Invertible Matrix Theorem. Left-multiplying both sides of equation (4) by $$\left( \underset{C\leftarrow B}{P} \right)^{- 1}$$ yields
$$\left(\right. \underset{C \leftarrow B}{P} \left.\right)^{- 1} \left[\right. x \left]\right._{C} = \left[\right. x \left]\right._{B}$$
Thus $$\left( \underset{C\leftarrow B}{P} \right)^{- 1}$$ is the matrix that converts $$C$$ -coordinates into $$B$$ -coordinates. That is,
$$\left(\left(\right. \underset{C \leftarrow B}{P} \left.\right)\right)^{- 1} = \underset{B \leftarrow C}{P}$$
section.heading: Change of Basis in ℝn
section.paragraph: If $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{n}} \right\}$$ and $$\varepsilon$$ is the standard basis $$\left\{ \mathbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{e}_{n} \right\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then $${\lbrack\mathbf{b}_{1}\rbrack}_{\varepsilon} = \mathbf{b}_{1}$$ , and likewise for the other vectors in $$B$$ . In this case, $$\underset{\varepsilon\leftarrow B}{P}$$ is the same as the change-of-coordinates matrix $$P_{B}$$ introduced in Section 4.4, namely
$$P_{B} = \left[\right. b_{ \text{1} } & b_{ \text{2} } & \ldots & b_{n} \left]\right.$$

To change coordinates between two nonstandard bases in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , we need Theorem 15. The theorem shows that to solve the change-of-basis problem, we need the coordinate vectors of the old basis relative to the new basis.

section.paragraph: Another description of the change-of-coordinates matrix $$\underset{C\leftarrow B}{P}$$ uses the change-of-coordinate matrices $$P_{B}$$ and $$P_{C}$$ that convert $$B$$ -coordinates and $$C$$ -coordinates, respectively, into standard coordinates. Recall that for each $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ ,

$$P_{B} \left(\left[\right. x \left]\right.\right)_{B} = x , & P_{C} \left(\left[\right. x \left]\right.\right)_{C} = x , & \text{and} & \left(\left[\right. x \left]\right.\right)_{C} = P_{C}^{- 1} x$$
Thus
$$\left(\left[\right. x \left]\right.\right)_{C} = P_{C}^{- 1} x = P_{C}^{- 1} P_{B} \left(\left[\right. x \left]\right.\right)_{B}$$

In $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the change-of-coordinates matrix $$\underset{C\leftarrow B}{P}$$ may be computed as $$P_{C}^{- 1}P_{B}$$ . Actually, for matrices larger than $$2 \times 2$$ , an algorithm analogous to the one in Example 3 is faster than computing $$P_{C}^{- 1}$$ and then $$P_{C}^{- 1}P_{B}$$ . See Exercise 22 in Section 2.2.
